activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
The morning of Grandpa Walt's funeral, Blake sat at the kitchen table with the newspaper open in front of him, pushing his eggs around the plate. Mom had said he could skip breakfast if he wanted, but he made himself take three bites anyway. At the bottom of the page he found a box with Grandpa's name at the top and a picture of him from years ago, back when his beard was still brown. Blake read it slowly, twice.

"It says here Grandpa was a sailor," he said. "On cargo ships. He never told me that."

Mom set down her coffee. "That's the obituary," she said. "It's a published notice that someone died, and it tells about their life. Family, work, what they loved."

Blake frowned at the paper. "But I saw him every summer for six years. He taught me checkers. He hated boats. He wouldn't even get in the paddle boat at the lake." It didn't make sense. Either the paper was wrong, or there was a whole part of Grandpa he had never seen, and that second possibility felt worse, like finding a hallway in a house you thought you knew.

He pushed the eggs away and decided he could not postpone figuring this out until after the funeral. He went to the pantry where Mom kept the old photo boxes, the ones Grandma had left behind, and dug through them while Mom dried dishes behind him. The first box was all babies and weddings. The second box was mostly blurry birthdays. Then, near the bottom, his fingers hit a stiff rectangle.

The photograph showed a man in a white uniform standing on a ship's deck, one hand on a railing, squinting into the sun. It was Grandpa. Young, skinny, and grinning like Blake had never seen him grin, not even when he won at checkers. Behind the photo, in pencil, someone had written: "Walt, first crossing, 1968."

"Mom," Blake called. "Come look at this."

She came over, wiped her hands on the towel, and when she saw the picture she sat down hard in the chair beside him. "I never saw this," she said quietly. "He never talked about it. Not once."

Blake turned the photo over, then back again. "Why wouldn't he talk about it?" he asked. "If I'd sailed across an ocean, I'd tell everybody. I'd tell the mailman."

Mom laughed a small, cracked laugh and put her hand on his shoulder. "Some people keep things," she said. "Maybe it hurt somewhere. Maybe he liked having one thing that was only his."

Blake had felt like despair was waiting for him all week, sitting in the corner of every room, but holding the photograph, something shifted instead. There was a version of Grandpa he had never met, and it wasn't a lie, it was a door. He slid the photo into the pocket of his dress pants, right over his heart, where it made a stiff little square against the fabric.

"Can I carry it into the church?" he asked.

"You carry it," Mom said, "all day."

story:
The baby had been crying for eleven minutes, which Emilia knew because she was watching the clock on the microwave the way other people watched horror movies. Her cousin Priya had gone to a movie with her parents, and Priya's neighbor Mrs. Okafor had asked if one of them could watch eight-week-old Theo for the evening. Priya had a play rehearsal. Emilia, who was visiting for the week and had never babysat anything larger than a hamster, had said yes mostly to have something to do.

For the first hour it had gone fine. Theo had slept, and Emilia had explored Mrs. Okafor's apartment, which smelled like lavender and had a fridge magnet shaped like a saxophone. Then Theo woke up and began to cry, and nothing worked. She fed him. She changed him, which was an experience she would not describe to anyone, ever. She walked him in circles, sang to him, burped him twice. The crying continued at a volume that seemed to obstruct all rational thought, filling the room so completely that she couldn't hear herself deciding what to try next.

She was standing in the kitchen, bouncing Theo harder and harder on her shoulder, her arms aching, when she noticed the folder of notes Mrs. Okafor had left on the counter. Emergency numbers, feeding times, and a page headed IMPORTANT, which Emilia read while Theo screamed into her collarbone. Never shake him, it said. A baby's neck muscles are too weak to support his heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury. If he cries and cries and you feel yourself getting frustrated, put him somewhere safe and step away for a minute. It's okay. Emilia stopped bouncing. Her arms had been doing something that felt, suddenly, like a bad idea from the future.

She carried Theo to his crib, set him down on his back, and walked to the far side of the room. He kept crying. She stood by the window, hands flat on the sill, and breathed until her shoulders came down from around her ears. It felt like breaking a treaty with herself, leaving him there, but the note had said it was okay, and the note knew more than she did. She texted Priya: "The baby has been screaming for 15 minutes. I put him in his crib and walked away like the note said. Is that normal or am I the worst babysitter in history?"

Priya's reply came fast: "totally normal. he does this. give it 5 min." Emilia watched the clock again, this time without dread. At minute four, Theo's cries slowed into hiccupy gulps. At minute five, the apartment went tranquil, all at once, like someone had lifted a lid off the room. She crept over and looked down. He was asleep, one fist against his cheek, red-faced and furious-looking even in defeat.

She sat on the floor beside the crib with the IMPORTANT page in her lap and read it again. Then she texted Priya one more line: "Tell Mrs. Okafor he slept from 8:40 to now, and I want hazard pay."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights died at 7:40, right in the middle of Colton's homework. He sat very still in his dark bedroom and waved a hand in front of his face. He could feel his fingers moving, but he could not see them at all. "Great," he said to nobody. "Blind and stuck on fractions."

In the living room his little sister Priya had already lit the emergency candle, and his dad was poking at the breaker panel by the door with his phone flashlight. "Nothing tripped," Dad reported. "Whole building must be out. Probably lost voltage on the whole block." Priya was busy drawing bees on construction paper by candlelight for a school poster. "Bees pollinate flowers," she announced. "That means they carry the powdery stuff around. My poster is going to be intricate. Like, super detailed." "Then you'll need more than one candle," Colton said, and she stuck her tongue out at him.

Colton went back for his phone and found the battery at four percent. He could not waste the flashlight, so he sat on the couch in the dark instead. That was when he noticed something strange. Ten minutes ago he could not even see his own hand. Now, when he waved it, he caught a pale blur against the darker blur of the wall. He turned toward the window, where a sliver of city glow leaked through the blinds, and slowly the coffee table appeared, then the edge of the armchair, then the intricate pattern of shadows the blinds threw across the floor.

"Okay, science experiment," he said out loud. "If I sit here even longer, can I see the whole room?" Priya scooted over to share the experiment, mostly because she wanted to be included. They sat side by side, not talking, staring into the dark while the minutes crawled by. The couch cushions grew clearer. The bookshelf separated itself from the wall. When Colton checked his phone, exactly half an hour had passed since the lights went out. He could make out the whole living room, soft and gray, like an old photograph. "Whoa," Priya whispered. "Our eyes are upgrading."

Colton remembered something his science teacher had mentioned once, about a pigment in the rod cells of the retina, and the word floated back to him. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It fades out when there's light, and in the dark your eyes rebuild it. Takes half an hour or more." He counted backward in his head and it matched, almost to the minute. "So the longer we sit here," Priya said slowly, "the better we see?" "That's the rule. Total darkness superpowers."

Then the lights snapped back on, blinding white, and both of them yelped and buried their faces in the couch pillows. From the doorway Dad laughed. "Congratulations, kids. Now your rhodopsin is toast." "Dad!" Priya shouted, eyes squeezed shut. "Turn it off, we weren't done with the experiment!"

story:
Arthur had been waiting for the farm field trip since September, mostly because of the old farmhouse. The bus bumped up a dirt lane between fertile fields, past cows that barely looked up, and stopped at a red barn where a guide in a straw hat was already waving. Arthur's teacher, Ms. Okafor, counted heads twice, then said the magic words: "The farmhouse is a museum now. Everything inside is over a hundred and fifty years old."

Inside, the rooms smelled like dust and wood smoke. Arthur drifted toward a wide oak desk near the window, the kind with little drawers and a worn leather top. His hand was almost on the edge, fingers an inch from the wood, when a girl named Priya grabbed his sleeve.

"Don't touch that!"

"Why not?" Arthur pulled his arm back. "It's just a desk. It looks strong."

"It is strong," Priya said. "That's not the problem. Museums ask visitors not to touch objects because oils and salts from your skin build up over time, and they can stain or damage the surfaces."

Arthur frowned. Oils and salts? From skin? His hand looked perfectly clean. He turned it over and studied his palm like it might be hiding something. Could something invisible really hurt a desk that had survived a century and a half of farmers? A question formed in his mind, the kind he liked best: if the oils and salts built up over time, wouldn't there be proof somewhere?

He wandered the room with his hands jammed in his pockets, looking for evidence. He noticed the banister on the staircase first. The middle of each rail was darker than the ends, a smooth brown stripe exactly where a hand would slide. The doorknob on the pantry door gleamed like a polished coin, while the hinges above it stayed dull and gray. On the desk itself, he leaned close without touching and saw that the front edge, the part a person's arm would rest on, had a soft shine the rest of the wood didn't have.

"There," he said to Priya, pointing. "Look at the banister. It's darker in the middle, right where hands go. And the doorknob's all shiny. That's years and years of hands, isn't it? That's the buildup." He was starting to grin. One kid touching the desk once wouldn't matter, the way one raindrop wouldn't flood a field. But a thousand hands, ten thousand, every one leaving a little behind? That was different. The damage wasn't one moment; it was a pattern, and patterns left marks.

Priya peered at the banister and nodded slowly. "I never thought about it like that."

Arthur still felt a small sting of resentment about the rule, if he was honest. His fingers itched to feel that old wood, and it seemed unfair that a desk could sit there begging to be touched and nobody was allowed. But now he understood the motive behind the sign by the door, the one that said PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH in curly letters. It wasn't about him being clumsy or careless. It was about what he couldn't see sitting on his skin.

At the end of the tour, the guide let them touch one thing, a rough iron horseshoe from the blacksmith shed, and Arthur held it with both hands, running his thumb over the rust. Even this, he realized, would slowly change under a million thumbs.

"Next museum," he told Priya as they climbed back on the bus, "I'm bringing a magnifying glass. I bet I can find the shiny spots from the front row seat."

The bus dropped Leo's class at the nature reserve just as a fire truck rolled up beside the visitor center, a low brick building donated years ago by an affluent family whose name was carved over the door. "Smoke machine today," said Ms. Ruiz, checking her clipboard. "The firefighters set up a demonstration in the classroom wing, and everyone goes through it."

Inside, a firefighter named Captain Osei explained the drill. A haze machine would fill the room with harmless gray vapor, and each student had to cross from the door to the far window and back. Leo watched the first group go. Priya stood up halfway, coughed on the fake smoke, and had to start over. Most kids walked, heads bent, and bumped into desks they couldn't see. When Leo's turn came, he crouched at the door and paused. The smoke hung in a thick layer above him, and down near the carpet the air looked strangely clear, like the space under a floating blanket. Was the cool air actually down there, or did it just look that way? He had a theory, and a way to test it: he pulled his sweatshirt sleeve over his nose and stood up slowly, inch by inch, like a periscope rising. At knee height, nothing. At waist height, the sleeve went gray and his eyes stung. He dropped back down and crawled the rest of the way, fast and clean, without touching a single desk.

"Best time so far," Captain Osei announced, squinting at her stopwatch. "Anyone know why he kept so low?"

"Because the smoke and heat rise," Leo said, "so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. That's why you taught us to crawl low under smoke." He pointed up at the thick gray ceiling of vapor. "I checked, kind of. I stood up slowly to verify where the clean part ended. It's like an invisible line."

"That's some solid logic," the captain said, grinning. "Though next time, verify with your hand, not your face."

That evening Leo wrote a letter to his grandfather, who used to volunteer at a fire station.

Dear Grandpa, You'll like this. Today we crawled through fake smoke at the nature reserve and I found out the clean air hides at the bottom. Everyone else walked through the gray cloud like confused ghosts. Priya says hi. Did you ever crawl for real? Write back and tell me.

A week later the answer came, in shaky handwriting: "Twice, kiddie. Both times the floor saved me. Stay low."

Leo read it twice, then taped it above his desk, right where he could see it from his bed.

story:
Dinner was lasagna, the good kind with the crunchy edges, and Paige pushed hers around the plate in slow circles. Tomorrow morning she had to stand up in front of the whole class and read her poem out loud, and even thinking about it made her stomach feel like it was full of ice water. Her hands were clenched in her lap under the table.

"You're not eating," said her older brother Dex, who was home from soccer practice and working on his third helping.

"I have anxiety about the poem thing," Paige said. "That's what Mom called it last time. My chest gets all tight and my heart goes fast."

Across the table, six-year-old Theo waved his fork. "I'm a herbivore," he announced, stacking his zucchini slices into a tower. "I only eat plants. And garlic bread."

"That's not how it works, but fine," said Dad, breaking a piece of bread that had gone brittle in the oven. It crackled and showered crumbs across the tablecloth.

Dex set down his fork. "You know what my coach has me do before a penalty shot? Goalies and penalty takers, both. You breathe in, then let it out slow, like twice as long as the in breath. Long exhales." He demonstrated, puffing the air out so his cheeks went flat. "It's a coping skill. Whole team does it before a stressful moment, before we even walk on the pitch. It calms the body's stress response down. That's what he said."

"Does it actually work?" Paige asked.

"Try it and see. Can't hurt."

She was quiet for a moment. It seemed strange that breathing could change anything, since breathing was just a thing her body did anyway, like blinking. But there was a way to test an idea, and she knew it. You did it and watched what happened, the same way you'd check whether the toaster was broken or just unplugged. She took a slow breath through her nose, counted to four, then let it out through her mouth, long and thin, like she was fogging a window gently.

"Feeling any better?" Dex asked.

"My heart's not going as fast," Paige said, surprised. She did it again, and this time she paid attention on purpose. In, slow. Out, slower. The ice water in her stomach didn't vanish, but it turned into something more like cold tap water, which she could live with.

Later, in her room with the poem cards spread on the bed, she tried to replicate the exact same thing, in through the nose for four, out for six or seven. She did it three times before practicing the first line out loud to her poster of the solar system. Her voice came out steadier than she expected, and she said the second line to her reflection in the mirror, and then the third.

"Boundaries," she told Mars on the poster, holding up a hand. "You don't get to hear the ending until tomorrow."

At breakfast she set her fork down, breathed in slow, and let the breath out long, watching it fog a little against the cold window. Then she picked up her poem cards and walked out the door.

story:
Rose had babysat plenty of toddlers before, but never a baby, and eight-month-old Ivy weighed almost nothing in her arms, like a bundle of laundry. She followed Mrs. Okafor's directions through the park to the shaded benches near the duck pond, where a stroller ride was supposed to knock Ivy out for her afternoon nap.

"There's a note in the diaper bag," Mrs. Okafor had said before leaving. "Please read it. It's important."

Ivy fell asleep on the third loop around the pond, her fists curled under her chin. Rose wheeled the stroller back toward the bench and dug out the note. The handwriting was small and careful: Back at two. Nap is at one. Safe sleep: on her back only, firm flat surface, no pillows, no blankets, no toys.

Rose frowned. The note sat on the bench beside the diaper bag, which was stuffed with a soft yellow blanket embroidered with a cartoon emperor penguin, its wings spread wide. Rose had planned to spread that blanket on the grass, lay Ivy on it, and tuck the edges around her like a nest. It looked so cozy. She had even imagined the penguin watching over Ivy like a little guard.

But the note said no blankets. And grass wasn't flat exactly, and it wasn't firm either, not the way a floor was firm. Rose looked at the blanket, then at the stroller seat. The stroller seat reclined all the way back until it lay flat, and it had a hard frame underneath. She pushed the lever, and the seat lowered with a click.

"Okay," Rose whispered to the sleeping baby. "You go on your back, on this, and Penguin stays in the bag." She lifted Ivy out slowly, the way you'd carry a full glass of water across a room, and lowered her onto the flat seat. Ivy's eyes stayed shut. Rose clicked the buckle across her, loose and gentle, then stepped back and checked from three angles that Ivy was still on her back. She was.

A woman on the next bench leaned over. "She'll be cold without a blanket, won't she?"

"Mrs. Okafor emphasized back sleeping on a firm, flat surface," Rose said, surprising herself with how steady she sounded. "No pillows, no blankets, no toys. Babies under one are safer that way." She pointed to the note. "It's all right here in her handwriting. I decided I'd rather follow it exactly than guess."

The woman nodded slowly. "I used to put mine on her stomach. That's what everyone did." She watched Ivy sleeping, pink-faced and undisturbed. "You're a careful one."

When Mrs. Okafor hurried back at five of two, Rose handed her the note, the blanket still folded, and the penguin still in the bag. "She slept forty whole minutes," Rose said. "On her back, on the flat seat, nothing in there but her."

Mrs. Okafor let out a breath and put both hands on Rose's shoulders. "Could you come back Thursday?"

story:
Jace noticed it at the fridge, where Marcus was standing with the door open without taking anything out. They had been friends since second grade, and Marcus never just stood at a fridge. He grabbed the juice, made a joke, kicked the door shut with his heel.

"You want a snack?" Jace asked.

"I'm not hungry." Marcus closed the fridge and sat down at the kitchen table. He pulled out his phone, then put it back. He picked up a pencil from the counter and tapped it against the wood, four taps, pause, four taps.

Jace sat across from him. Last week Marcus had skipped soccer practice, which he never did, and yesterday he had laughed at nothing Jace said, the fake kind of laugh that comes half a second too late. Jace had been building a theory in his head: something was wrong that Marcus wasn't saying out loud, and the pattern of small changes was the evidence.

In health class, their teacher had put up a poster and told them to read it themselves. Jace remembered the exact words because he'd copied them into his notebook for the quiz. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He'd assumed it was quiz material, nothing more. But standing there now, he thought about the "social" part. If friendships counted inside mental health, then what happened between him and Marcus wasn't separate from how Marcus was doing overall. It was part of the same thing.

"Remember in fourth grade," Jace said, "when you got picked for the county math team and your dad called it the most prestigious thing that ever happened to our family?" Marcus's dad had framed the certificate and hung it over the toaster.

Marcus almost smiled. "He still points at it when he makes eggs."

"And then the team got cut because the county ran out of budget, and you were fine about it."

"I wasn't fine," Marcus said. He set the pencil down. "I told everyone I was fine."

Jace waited. In his theory, the missing money part mattered too, so he asked, "Is it your dad's shop?" Marcus's dad repaired bicycles, and the whole spring had been slow. Marcus looked up fast, surprised, then nodded.

"The revenue's been down for months. They might lose the lease. If we move, I change schools." His voice went thin on the last word. "I didn't want to say it out loud because it gets bigger when I say it."

"That's backwards," Jace said. "Stuff gets smaller when you say it. That's how it works with my mom and her stress thing. She calls her breathing exercises coping, and she says I can borrow them if I ever need to."

"My sister says I have anxiety," Marcus said. "She read about it."

"Maybe. You could talk to the counselor about it, and you could also just talk to me. I'm asking for that. Consider it a boundary: no more fake laughs, and no more standing at the fridge pretending you're hungry."

Marcus opened the fridge, took out the juice, and poured two glasses.

The group chat lit up at 7:02 p.m., right after dinner. Maya had posted a screenshot of an email from their teacher, and beneath it, eleven people were typing at once. Ella scrolled through the chaos: someone sent a string of exclamation points, someone else typed in ALL CAPS, and Priya dropped a single thumbs-up. "Guys," Ella typed slowly, "nobody can even tell what we're deciding."

The problem was real. Maya's birthday was in nine days, and she wanted to invite the whole class, all twenty-six kids, by email instead of paper invitations this year. But nobody had everyone's address. Some kids had never shared theirs, and Maya refused to ask people to send their emails to the whole group. "It's not fair to just hand out everybody's address to everybody," she wrote. "My mom says that's how spam lists start."

Ella stared at her phone. She thought about the email her soccer coach sent every fall, the one listing practices and field locations. When she'd hit reply once, the message had gone only to the coach, not to all the other parents, and she'd noticed the To line was strangely short. Somewhere in that memory, a word persisted in nagging at her: three letters, hiding in plain sight near the top of the email form. She opened her own account and started a new message, typing Maya's address in the To field, then looking carefully at the little links beside it. Cc. Bcc.

She clicked Bcc and typed in her own address, then sent a test message to Maya: "Look at the To and Bcc lines and tell me what you see." Two minutes later Maya replied, and then posted in the group chat: "ELLA. This is it." She pasted a screenshot. Ella typed the explanation she'd worked out: "BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy.' People you add in the Bcc field still get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses." Maya added, "So I can put everybody in Bcc and nobody's address gets shared with everyone."

The plan still had wrinkles. Maya's first attempt failed because she'd typed half the class into the regular To line by accident, and Priya gently pointed it out: "Same problem, different window. Try again." Maya tried again, and this time the test email arrived in Ella's inbox with a To line showing only Maya's own address. It was like mailing twenty-six sealed envelopes instead of one giant postcard.

The next evening, the invitations went out. Every kid in class got one, and when Dylan replied asking who else was invited, Maya could honestly say he'd have to wait and see. "The mystery is part of the party," she wrote, and Ella laughed out loud at her desk. Then a new message appeared, from Maya only to her: "Chronic overthinker saves the day again. You're getting the first slice of cake." Ella grinned and typed back, "Deal. But I want it in writing."

Victor had one job at Marcus's birthday sleepover: find out where the new kid, Aiden, was from, so they could put it on the team sheet for the international food day. He waited until they were all sprawled on the living room floor with pizza, because asking at the door would have been rude.

My parents say home is Ohio, but I've never lived there longer than a summer." He shrugged. "I always get stuck on that question. It's like asking a fish which puddle it owns."

The other kids offered guesses. Marcus said Ohio, because that's where Aiden's parents were from. Priya said Singapore, because that's where he'd lived longest. Aiden shook his head at every answer, and Victor noticed his shoulders creeping up toward his ears. His own dad had moved from one country to another before Victor was born, and Victor had once overheard a phrase at his aunt's house. "My aunt says there's a name for kids like you," he said. "Third culture kid. An American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, made it up back in the 1950s. For kids raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Aiden turned around slowly. "Say the name again."

"Third culture kid."

Aiden said it back, once, then again, like he was trying on a coat that might actually fit. "So I'm not from nowhere. I'm from a third place, the one in between." He laughed, a real laugh this time. "It's a paradox, isn't it? The question made me feel like I had no answer, and the answer is that the in-between is the answer."

Victor wrote it down on the team sheet: Aiden, third culture kid, four countries. Priya read it over his shoulder and said they could make a dish from each place, a little buffet, and it would be the best table in the cafeteria, inevitable really, since no one else would have four flags.

Aiden grabbed the marker and drew a fifth flag with a question mark on it. "For the third culture," he said, and held it up for everyone to see.

story:
Autumn had exactly one week to get her science fair project ready, and her only idea was to smear mud on a baking sheet and hope for the best. She sat on her grandmother's porch steps with her chin in her hands, staring at the garden hose coiled by the fence.

"What's the sighing about?" Grandma asked, setting down two glasses of lemonade even though Autumn hadn't asked for any, which was typical.

"I have to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Erosion and deposition. It's mandatory for the unit grade, and I can't picture it. A canyon is huge and slow, and I can't even see time." She took the lemonade anyway, because refusing Grandma's lemonade was like refusing a sunrise.

Grandma tipped her head toward the hill behind the garden, where a shallow gully ran down past the compost bin to the creek. "You see that ditch? Your grandfather filled it in twice. Twice. That gully beat him like an old adversary. Every hard rain carved it right back out."

Autumn walked up the slope and crouched at the edge of the groove. It was maybe a foot deep, with pebbles heaped at the bottom where the water had dropped them, and at its mouth, where it met the flat ground, a little fan of mud spread out like a tiny delta. The water had carried dirt away here and dumped it there, and it had done it all without her ever once watching it happen. She grinned, turned the hose on low, and aimed it at the top of the gully.

For an hour she experimented. A trickle barely moved anything, so she pinched the nozzle and made a torrent, and the gully deepened so fast she actually yelped. Then she watched the fan of mud at the bottom grow, layer after layer, and thought about the Colorado River doing that not for an hour but for millions of years. At school they'd read that the Grand Canyon is 277 miles long, 446 kilometers if you measured that way, and over a mile deep at its deepest point. She'd skipped past that number before. Now she stood at the bottom of the garden, looked up at where she'd started at the top of the hill, and tried to picture a mile of rock going down instead of up. Her brain stuttered. A mile was a whole mile, straight into the ground, and the river had done it one rainy afternoon at a time.

"Grandma, was Grandpa really mad about the gully?" she called.

The argument started three rows from the back of the bus, which was where most good arguments started. Marcus held up his phone with the district cross-country standings. "Torrance is number one," he said. "Riverview's girl is second. Torrance is obviously faster."

"Obviously by how much?" Ella asked.

Marcus looked at her the way people look when a question is more trouble than it's worth. "By first place. That's the whole point of first place."

Eella wanted the standings for a reason of her own. Her brother Cole ran for Torrance, and their dad had watched the state meet on TV last spring, where the silver medalist in the hundred meters lost by less than a blink. Cole had moped about it for a week, saying the guy was basically as fast as the winner. Their dad, who considered himself Cole's mentor in all things running, had disagreed at dinner every night since. Ella intended to settle it, because she was optimistic about her chances of winning an argument nobody had asked her to join.

She leaned over the seat. "Rankings don't tell you the gap. Torrance's girl could be ahead by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute. First and second just tells you the order."

"You made that up," Marcus said.

"Then let's check." Coach Peters kept meet times on a clipboard that lived in the equipment shed, and Ella knew it came out of the shed every Thursday, when the equipment cart rolled onto the bus for away meets. Today was Thursday. When the cart rattled aboard at the next stop, she flipped the clipboard open on her knees while Marcus held the phone.

Torrance's top runner had run the two-mile in 11:42.06. Riverview's had run 11:42.07. One hundredth of a second. Marcus stared at the numbers, then at his phone, which said the same two names in the same order and nothing else.

"Okay," he said slowly, "but that's just those two."

She turned the page. Fifth place and sixth place in the standings were two kids from Farmington and Halloway. Their times were 12:10 and 13:05. Fifty-five seconds apart, and the ranking treated that gap exactly the same as the hundredth of a second, which was to say it didn't treat it at all.

Marcus wrote both pairs of numbers in the fog on the window with his finger, as if the glass might disagree too. The glass did not.

That night she told Cole, who took the news the way runners take hills. "So the guy on TV," he said, "could've been a hundredth behind. Or a minute." He picked up his shoes by the door. "I'm going to go run the same time as somebody faster than me."

story:
Brooklyn sat in the back seat of the family car with a paper bag from the eye doctor's office folded on her lap. Inside was her first pair of glasses, and she hadn't put them on yet. "You could try them now," her dad said from the driver's seat. "We're stuck in traffic anyway."

"Give me a minute," Brooklyn said. She was thinking about how she'd figured it out in the first place. Last month she'd been in the back row of science class, copying the board through a fog of blurry letters, while her phone screen an inch from her nose stayed sharp as anything. That made no sense, so she'd run a test. She'd made a hole in a piece of paper with the point of a pencil, held it up to one eye, and looked at the board through it. The letters sharpened. She'd tried the same trick at home with her phone, and it barely changed anything, which meant the problem was with faraway stuff, not near stuff. She'd marched that paper to the eye doctor and asked him why it worked.

He'd looked at the little hole and laughed. "Clever. In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it. Your eyeball is slightly too long, that's all." He'd tapped a diagram on the wall, and she'd traced the light rays with her finger, meeting too soon and smearing the picture before it ever reached the back of her eye. The paper hole had blocked the sloppy rays, she guessed, letting only the neat ones through. It was like her eye was a camera built one millimeter wrong, and a hole could pretend it wasn't.

"I'm going to look like a librarian," she said now, "or like an artisan who makes tiny violins for mice."

"An artisan of tiny violins," her dad said gravely. "There's a future in that. Now open the bag before I have to pull over."

She slid the glasses on. The world converted itself all at once, the way a blurry photo snaps into focus. She could read the license plate of the truck three cars ahead. She could count the exits still to come. She could see, far down the highway, a billboard that she'd only ever known as a pink smudge. "Dad. Dad, that sign says EXIT ONLY."

"I've known that sign my whole life, Brook."

"It has a little arrow on it. It has always had a little arrow." She pressed her forehead against the window and stared out at everything, wide awake after months of feeling lethargic in class, half asleep behind her own eyes. "Can we take the long way home? There's a hawk or a garbage bag on that pole, and I need to know which."

The end-of-season party was supposed to be the fun part, but by the time the pizza boxes were half empty, Charlotte noticed that nobody was eating much. Her soccer team, the Parkside Foxes, sat in a loose circle under the pavilion, and everyone kept glancing around like they were counting heads. Marisol was moving pepperoni slices into rows. Benji had his cleats off and was staring into them. Charlotte had been looking forward to this all week, and now the whole thing felt heavy, like the air before a storm that never arrives.

"We lost the tournament," Benji said finally. "That's not why it's weird, though."

"I know," Marisol said. "It's weird anyway."

Charlotte pulled her phone out of her bag, pretending to check the time. What she actually did was search: why does a team feel sad at the end of a season even when nothing bad happened. She scrolled past a bunch of advice columns until she hit a page about how groups develop. Four stages, a man named Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing. Then she read the line that made her sit up straight. In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.

"Listen to this," she said, out loud, before she could decide not to. "It's a real thing. There's a fifth stage and it's called adjourning."

Marisol looked up. "What does that mean?"

"It's the part where the team ends." Charlotte held the phone so they could see the screen, her thumb covering an ad. "In 1977, Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added it to the other four stages. So this horrible feeling is, like, documented."

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Benji laughed, short and surprised. "You mean everybody gets this? Not just us?"

"Everybody. Every group."

Marisol stopped rearranging the pepperoni. "So we're not falling apart. We're just in the last stage."

The knot in Charlotte's chest loosened a little. It wasn't that the sad feeling went away, exactly. It was more like the feeling had a name now, and named things were smaller than nameless things. She noticed, too, that a low-grade resentment she'd been carrying all afternoon, about her dad showing up late and missing her only goal of the whole season, faded at the same time. Hard to stay mad about small stuff when the whole team was going through an official stage together.

"There's a wasp by the juice," Priya announced, and everyone scrambled. The wasp circled the cups with a predatory patience while five girls armed themselves with paper plates. Charlotte swatted and missed, and the wasp emitted a sharp buzz and looped up through the pavilion rafters, where it hovered like it was thinking it over.

"Next year," Marisol said, watching it go, "we might not all be on the same team. Tryouts get shuffled."

"We're not next year yet," Charlotte said. She stood up on the bench and put two fingers in her mouth and whistled at the whole pavilion. "Everybody grab a slice. We still have a stage to finish."

story:
The departure board at Gate 14 flicked from ON TIME to BOARDING, and Jeremy's dad picked up the biggest suitcase before anyone else could grab it. They were flying east across six hours of time zones, which meant that when they landed in the morning, their bodies would still believe it was the middle of the night. Jeremy knew this the way he knew his locker combination, as a fact he'd been told, not something he'd ever felt. His little sister, Priya, was already asking whether the hotel had a pool, and Mom was saying that she'd had to enroll Priya in the kids' activity club before they even left home, because the good spots filled up fast.

The flight was long and pale. Jeremy watched the little airplane on the screen crawl across the map, and he did the arithmetic in his head: six hours forward, so their arrival at nine in the morning would feel like three in the morning. When they landed, everyone was groggy except Priya, who had slept the whole way and bounced through the terminal like it was noon. "I'm starving," she announced. Jeremy's stomach, which knew perfectly well it was three in the morning, said nothing at all.

The first night in the hotel, everyone fell asleep at eight, local time, exhausted. That was fine. The second night was the strange one. At midnight, Jeremy lay in the dark listening to his dad turn over, and his mom sigh, and Priya whisper from the other bed that she was wide awake. Nobody could sleep. It didn't make sense to Jeremy, because they had all been tired, and it was night, and the room was dark and quiet. Something invisible was holding them all upright at midnight, and he wanted to know what rule it followed.

On the third night, Jeremy ran a quiet experiment. He noted the time when each of them finally dropped off. Priya went out around one. He himself fell asleep close to two, he thought, though he couldn't be sure, since being asleep made it hard to record. His parents were still murmuring when he went under. On the fourth night it was earlier, maybe one o'clock for him and midnight-ish for Priya. He wrote the numbers in the back of his notebook, and by the fifth night a pattern had crawled onto the page: each night, sleep arrived roughly an hour earlier than the night before.

He counted on his fingers. Six hours of time difference, one hour of catch-up per day. "So it takes about six days," he said at breakfast, spreading his notebook on the table. "One day for every hour of difference. That's why we were all awake at midnight on day two, and why Priya's getting normal faster than Mom and Dad, because she adjusts quicker than the average." Priya stole a piece of his toast and studied the columns. "Then tonight is night six," she said. "We should be fixed."

They took a family vote on how to spend the last difficult evening, and it was unanimous: early dinner, no screens, everyone in bed by ten. Jeremy lay in the dark and waited to see whether his rule held. Somewhere below, a taxi honked, and Priya's breathing slowed beside him, and then, without noticing the exact moment it happened, he was asleep.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
story:
The sign at Kwik Fuel read "Bottled Water $1.25" on Monday, and Mya rode past it without a second thought. By Thursday, after the storm knocked out the town's water pump, the same sign read "$4.00," and a hand-lettered note under it said "LIMIT 3 PER CUSTOMER." She stood in front of the cooler with five dollars in her pocket and did the math twice, because the first answer made her mad.

Her little brother Dez needed the water more than she did. Their mom had said to buy whatever she could on the way home from school, so Mya took three bottles and got in line behind a man buying an entire case at the new price without even blinking. "Four dollars," the cashier said. "It was a dollar twenty-five on Monday," Mya said. "Storm," the cashier said, as if that were a whole sentence. Ahead of her, the man with the case shrugged and paid, and two more people came through the door heading straight for the cooler.

At school that week, her social studies class had argued about a question on a worksheet: "Why is water cheap and a diamond expensive?" A boy named Teo had waved his pencil and said it was because diamonds are prettier, and Mya had not been able to come up with anything better. The teacher had written a hint on the board: In "The Wealth of Nations," published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal. Mya had copied it down because it would probably be on a quiz, not because she understood it.

Standing at the register, she understood it. Water was the most useful thing in the store today, everyone in town wanted it, there were only about forty bottles left in the cooler, and the price had jumped to four dollars. Teo's answer had the cause backwards. The price didn't rise because water had become prettier. It rose because it had become scarce, and a line of people stood behind her proving it. She thought about the diamonds in the glass case at the jewelry store downtown, tiny things in a locked box, expensive because there were almost none of them. The town pump, on the other hand, usually pushed out all the water anyone could use, which had to be part of why a bottle used to cost a dollar twenty-five.

She decided to test the idea, because a worksheet answer was one thing and real life was another. "If the pump gets fixed," she asked the cashier, "will the price go back down?" The cashier looked up from the register. "Happened after the ice storm two years ago. Price drops when the delivery trucks come back and I got shelves full of it. Nobody pays four bucks for something there's a wall of." He rang her up. "Twelve dollars even, since you got three."

Mya counted it out and incorporated the change into her plan: two bottles for drinking, one held back for the soup her mom wanted to make. On the walk home she passed the jewelry store, where a diamond the size of a peppercorn sat on velvet with a price that would have bought every bottle in the gas station. In the window's reflection, the store's weekly revenue probably came from a handful of tiny stones, while the gas station made its money on coffee, chips, and, this week, water. Two businesses, two completely distinct ideas about what a thing was worth, both of them right.

On Saturday the pump came back on, and Mya rode her bike to Kwik Fuel just to check. The sign said "$1.25." The cooler was packed, the delivery truck was idling out front, and nobody was in line. She went in and bought one bottle, mostly for proof, and the cashier nodded at it. "Told you."

story:
Juliette smoothed her skirt and followed her mother up the wide steps of the gurdwara, where her friend Simran's family had invited them for the celebration of Vaisakhi. She had never been inside one before, and she was doing her best not to stare at everything at once. Inside, the hall glowed with golden cloth and the smell of something warm and bready drifted from a doorway on the left.

"Cover your head," her mother whispered, handing her a thin scarf. Juliette wrapped it awkwardly and tucked her shoes onto a shelf beside dozens of others.

In the main hall they sat on the carpet behind Simran's family, listening to the music. Juliette understood only that it was beautiful, the harmonium humming under voices that rose and fell together. Her stomach growled during a long, eloquent chant, and she pressed her hand against it, embarrassed, until Simran leaned back and whispered, "Hungry? Good. Come on."

Simran led her down a corridor to a vast room where long rows of people sat cross-legged on the floor, side by side, families and strangers and an elderly man in a wheelchair all in the same lines. Volunteers moved between the rows carrying steel buckets. One paused beside Juliette, and before she could speak, a woman had set a steel tray in front of her, then a bowl of dal, then a cup of water.

Juliette caught Simran's sleeve. "Where do I pay? I didn't bring any money."

"You don't pay," Simran said, grinning. "It's called langar. It's a free meal for every visitor, no matter who you are."

"Everybody here?" Juliette looked down the row. A woman in jeans sat beside a grandfather in a turban sat beside a girl in a school uniform. "Even people who aren't Sikh? Even me?"

"Even you." Simran's grandmother, two places down, nodded as if she had heard, and Juliette realized she had probably asked too loudly. Her ears went hot, but nobody seemed offended. If anything, the volunteers looked pleased to have someone new to feed.

Juliette tested it anyway, quietly, in her own way. When the roti came, she asked the boy carrying the bucket for a second one, half expecting him to hesitate or check with someone. He just handed it over and moved on. She ate both, thoughtfully, watching the whole system work. Nobody paid, nobody was turned away, nobody sat above anyone else; everyone was down on the same carpet together, conserving nothing but space, each person scooting over to make room for the next.

When her tray was empty, she stood up and found the boy by the bucket. "Can I help?" she asked. He looked at her tray, then handed her a stack of fresh rotis wrapped in cloth, warm as a sleeping cat.

"Walk the rows," he said. "Give until your cloth is empty, then come back."

Juliette walked slowly, offering roti to each person with both hands the way she had seen him do it. The grandfather in the turban took one and said something to her in Punjabi that made the whole row smile. She didn't understand a word of it, but she understood the smile, and she kept walking, her cloth lighter with every step, until there was one roti left and she placed it in the hands of the girl in the school uniform, who bowed her head and whispered, "Thank you."

Piper sat on the low wall by the swings, her left arm stiff inside a bright green cast, and watched the others run the obstacle course she could not join. Three days ago she had decided that jumping off the top of the climbing dome was worth it, and now she had five weeks of sitting still to evaluate that decision. It did not look good so far.

"Green suits you," said Marcus, plopping down beside her. "I wanted orange." He tapped his own cast, the old one, pale blue and full of signatures, on his right leg. "I keep thinking about what Ms. Reyes said at the assembly, when the nurse asked if anyone knew how casts were invented. I raised my hand and got it wrong."

"You did not," Piper said.

"I said casts were invented in America in like 1900. Nobody knew anything, so we all just guessed." Marcus shrugged. "After school I looked it up. A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852. Before that, people wrapped broken arms in stiff stuff that didn't hold its shape the way plaster does."

Piper turned that over. "So every kid who ever broke an arm before 1852 got the wobbly version."

"Basically."

The bell had not rung yet, and a small crowd was gathering near the fence, where two fourth graders were arguing about whose paper airplane had flown farther. "We'll ask them," Marcus said. "We'll be the jury. Whichever one we pick has to be the winner."

Piper followed him over, holding her casted arm like something fragile and precious. She had not felt fragile before the jump. She had felt certain, which was worse.

The fourth graders, Sam and Bea, each held a plane and a grudge. Piper made them throw again, three times each, and she watched where each plane landed rather than how pretty it looked in the air. Bea's went farther twice. Sam's folded once and dropped like a stone. "Bea wins," Piper announced. "Two out of three."

Sam scowled at his plane. "It's the wind's fault."

"It's the same wind for both of you," said Marcus.

Sam studied the plane for a long moment, then walked to the fence and threw it one more time, watching carefully where it came down. Piper watched too. "Try it backwards," she called out. "Sam, throw it backwards and see if it still curves."

Everly had guessed something was wrong in October, when the words on the whiteboard began to blur unless she squinted. By November she had copied half her notes from the girl next to her, and her mother finally made an appointment. Now she sat in the waiting room of the optometrist's office, holding a slip of paper with her name on it while a machine hummed behind the door.

A boy about eight years old sat across from her, swinging his legs and staring at his own paper as if it might bite him. "Do you know what OD means?" he asked. "It says it right here. Twice." He held the paper out. "And the other one says OS. My sister says they're codes for what's wrong with you. Like a secret diagnosis. My aunt had a paper like this and then she had surgery."

Everly looked at her own slip. Under her name it said OD and OS, each followed by a row of numbers and plus signs. She didn't feel scared, exactly, but the letters did look official, the kind of thing that could hide something. She wanted to know before the doctor called her back, because if the codes meant something bad, she'd rather find out now than standing under the bright lights in the exam room.

She turned the paper over and thought. The letters came in pairs, one line for each. She covered her right eye with her hand, the way she did when she copied the board, and then her left. Two eyes, two lines. If OD and OS each stood for one eye, then the pair had to split left and right somehow. She looked around the room. On the wall hung a poster of an eye chart labeled with the same letters, and beside it a smaller chart of Latin roots for a vocabulary program the office ran with the school. OD could be oculus something. Right, in Latin, was dexter. She'd seen the word dexterity in a spelling list, and right-handed people were called dexterous. So OD was the right eye. That left OS, and sinister had come to mean something dark, but her social studies teacher had mentioned that in Latin it just meant left.

"OD is your right eye," she told the boy. "OS is your left. Oculus dexter, oculus sinister. It's just Latin."

"Latin? Not a code?" The boy looked at his paper again, and his legs stopped swinging. "So mine are just telling which eye is which?"

"That's all it's doing," Everly said. The fear in his face diminished by about half, and then the rest went when the receptionist called his name and it turned out he was only there for a checkup.

When it was Everly's turn, the doctor slid the new glasses onto her face. The room sharpened all at once, and the eye chart across from her showed letters she could name down to the smallest row. Through the open door she saw the boy leaving with his mother, and he waved his paper at her like a flag.

"Hey," he called across the waiting room. "My right eye is the good one. OD. I'm going to tell my sister her code theory is wrong."

story:
Asher had predicted that a marble rolling down a taller ramp would travel farther across the kitchen floor, and for three days the marble had stubbornly refused to agree with him. The ramp made of an old bookshelf board leaned against the counter at four different heights, and every time he raised it, the marble flew off the end, bounced once, and stopped in almost the same spot. His data sheet, which he had decorated with a drawing of the marble wearing a tiny helmet, now showed four nearly identical measurements.

"You look like somebody deleted your game save," said his sister Priya from the doorway, chewing a granola bar.

"My hypothesis is wrong." Asher flattened the data sheet against the table. "The whole poster says taller ramp, longer distance. If I present this, I'll embarrass myself in front of everyone."

Priya picked up the marble and rolled it across the table, watching it drop off the edge. "Maybe the floor is the problem. Or maybe the marble is just lazy."

Asher laughed, but then he stopped. He tried the ramp on the hallway's wooden floor instead of the kitchen tile. Same result. He tried a heavier marble. Same result, so close it was practically the equivalent of a photocopy of the first one. Whatever was happening, it wasn't a fluke, and it wasn't the floor. Something he couldn't see was keeping the distance the same, and that made him almost more curious than being right would have.

At school the next morning he cornered Ms. Okafor before homeroom. "My results prove my prediction wrong. Should I start over with a different project?"

"A result that shows your hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it's worth reporting," she said, handing him a fresh poster board.

He stared at it. "So I just... show everyone I was wrong?"

"You show everyone what you found."

That reframing felt like a metaphor for something, though Asher couldn't decide what. At home that evening he rebuilt the poster from scratch. The title now read, in letters he traced twice so they'd look bold: "WHY I WAS WRONG AND WHAT THE MARBLE KNOWS THAT I DON'T." He taped up the data sheet, drew an arrow to the suspiciously matching measurements, and added a question in red marker: "What hidden factor keeps the distance the same?" Maybe the marble lost speed somewhere he wasn't measuring. Maybe the board itself was doing something. He had questions, and somehow that felt better than having answers.

On science fair day, Priya found him at his table, straightening the marble helmet drawing for the tenth time. A kid from another class squinted at the poster and asked, "Wait, so your project is you being wrong?"

Asher slid the marble down the ramp one more time, and they both watched it roll to the exact spot where it always stopped.

story:
Matthew had been waiting all week for this, and now the whole living room at Mr. Alvarez's house smelled like chili and popcorn, and the pregame show was finally counting down. He grabbed the best seat, the beanbag chair closest to the giant TV, before his cousin Dana could claim it. Mr. Alvarez carried in a bowl of chips the size of a kiddie pool. "This is the year," he announced, "that my team finally goes all the way."

The doorbell rang twice more before kickoff. First came Mrs. Okafor from next door with her famous seven-layer dip, then Mr. Alvarez's brother with his dog, Biscuit, who immediately tried to steal a napkin. Everyone crowded onto the couch, and Matthew's little sister, Priya, squeezed in beside him. On the screen, the announcers kept saying the same phrase over and over: Super Bowl LVIII. "Wait," Priya said, squinting at the logo. "Why are there letters in the title? Where are the numbers?"

Matthew started to answer, then stopped, because he honestly didn't know. LVIII. He knew it was Roman numerals, the kind they carved on old buildings, but why would a football game use them? He thought maybe someone just thought they looked fancy, like when restaurants call a small drink "petite." Dana shrugged when he asked her. Mr. Alvarez's brother said, "Always been that way, I figure." That answer itched at Matthew the way a loose tooth did. Things that had always been a certain way had still started somewhere.

During the first quarter, Matthew borrowed Mr. Alvarez's tablet from the counter and searched for the very first one. He found it fast, and his mouth actually fell open. He tapped Priya on the shoulder. "You're not going to believe this. The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game."

Priya gasped like he'd revealed a magic trick. "Then where did 'Super Bowl' come from?" Matthew scrolled a little further, grinning. "The Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later. Somebody went back and stuck it on." Priya stared at the screen, then at the TV, then back. "So when they say LVIII, they're counting from a game that didn't even have that name?"

"Exactly!" Matthew said, louder than he meant to, and half the room turned. Mr. Alvarez held up a chip like a microphone. "The beanbag chair has an announcement."

Matthew stood up. "The first Super Bowl wasn't called the Super Bowl at all. It was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game, and the Roman numeral one came later." Dana whooped. Priya clapped. Even Biscuit barked, which made the dip wobble dangerously.

On the screen, the halftime show erupted in fireworks. Mrs. Okafor said the year her team lost the big game, she was so upset she let her mood deteriorate for a full week and wouldn't even watch highlights. Mr. Alvarez laughed and said that kind of thinking was toxic, and that tonight, win or lose, everyone was staying for ice cream sundaes. Priya leaned over to Matthew and whispered, "Next year, I'm going to know what the letters say before you do."

"Deal," Matthew said, and shook her hand, chili still on his fingers, as the second half kicked off and the whole room roared.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Jake sat at the kitchen table with his notebook open to a page that had only two sentences on it. His pencil hovered, then wrote a third, then stopped. His story was about a kid named Marcus who wanted to win the science fair, but nothing was going wrong for Marcus, and Jake knew that meant nothing was happening at all.

His little sister Nora slid into the other chair with a bowl of cereal and read over his shoulder. "Who's the bad guy?" she asked.

"There isn't one," Jake said. "That's the problem."

"Every story has one." She crunched her cereal like this was obvious.

Jake tapped his pencil against the table. He thought about the word he'd copied from the board at school: protagonist. The protagonist was a story's main character, and the antagonist was the character or force working against them; their conflict drove the plot toward the climax. He had assumed the antagonist had to be a villain in a black mask, something sinister with a cackle and a hidden lair. But the word "force" was sitting right there in his notes, and he kept stepping over it.

He looked at his story again. Marcus wanted to win the science fair. What worked against Marcus? Jake flipped back a page and found his answer: the weather forecast. A snowstorm was coming on the night of the fair, and if the school closed, Marcus would never get to show his project.

Jake sat up straight. "Nora, my antagonist is a snowstorm."

"That's not a person," she said.

"It doesn't have to be. It just has to fight him."

He started writing fast. First he had to calibrate the trouble, like tuning a radio to the right station, so the storm grew from a small worry to a real threat without jumping too soon. At the kitchen window the afternoon light was already going gray, and fat flakes had begun to stick to the glass, which felt like the storm was reading over his shoulder too.

He wrote the dialogue out carefully, checking every comma and quotation mark. "We can still make it," Marcus said. Then he built the climax: Marcus carrying his project through the snow to the school, the doors still open, the judges waiting.

When he finished, Jake read the last page aloud. Nora pushed her empty bowl aside. "So do they call a truce, Marcus and the storm?"

"No," Jake said. "Marcus wins." He underlined the final line, and outside, the real snow kept falling.

story:
Felix's new phone arrived in a box no bigger than a sandwich, and he tore it open on the kitchen table before Dad had even set down his coffee. The screen lit up blue, and Felix grinned at it like it was a door with no locks on the far side. He spent the whole afternoon setting it up, typing in his email password twice, and downloading a game about repairing lighthouses.

That evening, while he was charging the phone beside his bed, it buzzed. A message filled the screen: "Your login code is 471-208. If you didn't request it, ignore this message." Felix stared at the numbers. He hadn't typed his password anywhere since that afternoon. So who had? Somebody, somewhere, must have just tried to get into his account, and the only way to reach that gate was with his password. His stomach did a slow flip.

He ran downstairs holding the phone like evidence. "Dad, I got a code and I didn't ask for one."

Dad leaned in. "That's two-factor authentication," he said. "Good thing you turned it on."

Felix paced the kitchen, thinking out loud. "So the code is a second thing you have to show. It comes right to my phone. Even if somebody stole my password, that alone wouldn't be enough to get in. They'd be stuck at the door without this." He waved the phone. Then he stopped pacing, because a worse thought arrived. "Dad. Somebody has my password. That's the only way they could have triggered a code at all."

They sat at the table and changed it together, and Felix made the new one long and strange, a string no anonymous stranger on the internet would ever guess. Then he thought about where the old password could have leaked. He'd used the same one on a quiz site months ago, a site with pop-up ads that had eventually made him abandon it entirely. That had to be it. His old password, floating around out there like a key somebody found on the sidewalk.

The next morning Felix was ready with a plan, eager to test it. He asked Dad to try logging into the email account from the family laptop using the old password, just to see what happened. Dad typed it in, and a message popped up on Felix's phone: a new code request. The screen on the laptop said, "Enter the code sent to your device."

"See?" Felix said, bouncing on his toes. "The password got them one step in, and then they hit the wall. Without my phone, they're a civilian locked outside."

Dad laughed and closed the laptop. Felix picked up his phone and typed a note to himself, out loud as he wrote: "Rule one, unique password for every account." He read it twice, then held the phone up like a tiny trophy. "Lighthouse level two, here I come."

story:
The annual Marín family picnic had one rule that everybody ignored: bring a dish from your side of the family. Anthony had brought potato salad, which was from nobody's side, and it was already half gone. He was standing near the horseshoe pit when his cousin Dario and Dario's friend Sam started arguing, which was normal, except this time it wasn't about the score.

"Your grandma's from the rez but you live in the city," Sam said, flicking a horseshoe so it landed nowhere near the stake. "You can't just decide you're Native. Somebody has to, like, certify you."

"Certify me?" Dario picked up the other horseshoe. "Who, you?"

Anthony had been thinking about something similar all morning, ever since Great-Aunt Rosa had pinned him by the lemonade and listed every group she belonged to, which took a while, including two she invented herself. Nobody had ever told Rosa what she was. Rosa told you what she was, and then she told you what you were, and then she gave you more lemonade.

"Maybe there's an actual answer," Anthony said. "Like a rule about who decides."

Sam rolled his eyes. "There's no rule. You're so gullible."

But Anthony was already typing on his phone, one-handed so he wouldn't drop his plate. He found it faster than he expected, a United Nations document, and he read the part out loud. "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007." He scrolled. "It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

"Meaning what?" Dario said.

"Meaning the group decides who's in the group. Not Sam."

Sam made a face like the potato salad had turned on him. "Fine, but does a picnic count? This isn't, like, a council."

"It's Dario's family," Anthony said. "Seems like it counts more than horseshoes."

Later, Anthony told Rosa about the argument while she refilled his cup. She said that in her day people didn't look things up, they just argued longer, and that a good argument could spread through a family like a virus if nobody stopped it. Then she said he should prioritize eating over officiating disputes, since the refereeing didn't pay and the brisket was going fast.

Dario walked over with two forks and handed one to Sam, who took it after a strategic pause. "So membership committee," Sam said, mouth full. "That's a thing now?"

"That's a thing," Dario said, and pointed his fork at the dessert table.

story:
Alice discovered the lines in the bathroom mirror that morning, two thin pale streaks curving along her hip like someone had drawn them with a very fine pencil while she slept. She had pulled her waistband down twice to check, then three times, as if they might change their minds and vanish. Now she sat in the back seat of the family car with her sweatshirt tied around her waist, even though the heater was making the whole car smell like dusty warm air.

"Seatbelt," her dad said, glancing in the mirror. He was driving her to swim practice, and her little brother Ben was buckled in beside her, chewing a granola bar with his mouth open.

She buckled it, slowly. The problem was the swimsuit. In twenty minutes she would have to stand on a pool deck in front of the whole team, and the suit sat exactly where the lines were. Maybe she could claim she felt sick. The idea gave her a small twist of guilt, because it would be a lie, and Dad had already given up his Saturday morning to supervise her practices all season. He'd told her last week that his old stopwatch had become obsolete now that the team used electronic timers, but he still came anyway, clicking his dead watch out of habit.

"Hey, Dad," she said, watching the wipers push rain across the glass. "When you were twelve, did you ever grow really fast? Like, fast enough to notice?"

"Notice how?" He turned down the radio.

"Like, overnight. Clothes not fitting. Stuff."

He laughed. "Your uncle Matt grew four inches one summer. Why, are your jeans too short again?"

Alice hesitated. Ben was staring out the window, counting horses in the fields. "There are these lines," she said, quieter. "On my hips. Thin ones. I thought maybe something was wrong."

The car slowed at a light. "What do they look like?"

"Like little scratches that don't hurt. Pale."

Dad tapped the wheel, then reached over and turned the radio down the rest of the way. "You know what, your mom has some. I remember noticing them years ago, and she said everybody in her family got them. Want me to ask her at pickup?"

At the pool, Alice changed in the corner stall with the door locked, then stood there a long minute. Finally she pulled the suit strap up on her shoulder and walked out. Nobody looked. Nobody pointed. The pool smelled like chlorine and coconut shampoo, and the water was that impossible blue that made everything seem fine.

After practice, Mom was in the driver's seat with the heater running. She looked at Alice's hip for exactly five seconds and then smiled. "Stretch marks," she said. "Half the girls your age have them. Mine showed up during my big growth spurt, and they fade over time."

Alice buckled in and pressed her palm flat against her hip through the fabric. "So they're just... from growing?"

"Fast growing," Mom said, pulling out of the lot. "You shot up two sizes this year."

Alice leaned her head against the cold window and watched the rain. Maybe by next summer they'd be nearly invisible, and she'd be taller, and her jeans would be too short again.

"I'm ordering new jeans," she announced.

"Large ones," said Ben, and threw his granola bar wrapper at her head.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Bennett had earned a reputation on the fourth floor as the kid who grew tomatoes in a bucket, and this spring he intended to top it. He filled four flower boxes for the balcony railing with potting soil and planted beans, peas, lettuce, and peppers. His little sister Dot watched from the sliding door with a bag of chips. "Beans are boring," she said. "Peppers are boring. Plant candy."

"Beans are the smart choice," Bennett said, and patted the soil. He had read one sentence about them in a library book and it had stuck in his head, though he didn't entirely understand it yet.

For three weeks he was diligent about watering, checking every morning before school and again at dinner. The lettuce came up spindly and yellowish. The peppers sat there doing almost nothing. But the beans and peas shot up so fast they needed strings to climb, and by June the boxes were crowded with vines. Dot came out one evening, chewing, and frowned at them. "Why are the bean ones winning?" she asked.

That was the question Bennett had been circling all month. He had a guess, but a guess wasn't the same as knowing, so he decided to test it. He pulled up one scraggly pepper plant, shook the dirt off its roots, and looked. Smooth roots, white and skinny. Then, feeling a little guilty, he tugged up one bean plant from the crowded box. Its roots were covered in small lumps, dozens of them, like beads on a string. "Would you look at that," he said.

Dot leaned over. "Those bumps are weird. Is it sick?"

"They're called nodules," Bennett said, remembering the word from the book. "The book said beans and peas have bacteria in these little lumps, and the bacteria take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use." He held the root up to the porch light. The pepper had no bumps and no luck. The bean had both. That wasn't proof exactly, but it fit, and he anticipated that the peas would show the same thing. He pulled one pea vine, and there they were, the same small lumps. He grinned so wide Dot backed up a step.

"So the beans are cheating," Dot said.

"They're not cheating, they're farming." Bennett pushed the plants back into the soil, watered them, and propped the strings straight. He had been planning to pull the peas out to give the peppers more room, since peppers were the impressive crop, the one worth bragging about. He changed his mind on the spot. "Next year, this whole balcony is beans," he said, and went inside to find a marker and the back of Dot's chip bag, which was, he'd decided, the perfect place to draw the plan.

story:
Grace slammed the oven door shut and pulled out the third pan of the afternoon. The cookies looked wrong again, thick and dry, more like little cakes, and she winced when she broke one open and saw the crumbly middle. Her grandmother's kitchen smelled like butter and cinnamon, which was the only good news.

"I don't get it," Grace said, dropping into a chair. "I followed Grandma's recipe exactly. Twice."

Her grandmother set down her tea and slid the old recipe card across the table. Grace had copied it out that morning, one cup of flour, half a cup of sugar, one egg, all in her neatest handwriting. She had even made an amendment to the bottom of her copy: bake ten minutes, not twelve, because the first batch had burned.

"Show me how you measure the flour," her grandmother said.

Grace marched to the counter, grabbed her cup, and plunged it straight into the flour bag. She packed it full, tapped it level, and held it up like proof. "See? Perfectly full."

Her grandmother smiled, but not in a mean way. "Try it again. Only this time, weigh what's in the cup."

They dug out the old kitchen scale from under the sink, the one with the dial that Grandpa used for his coffee. Grace scooped another cup the same way and set it on the scale. Then her grandmother fluffed the flour with a spoon, spooned it gently into a fresh cup, leveled it with a knife, and weighed that too.

Grace leaned over the dial. "Mine's heavier. A lot heavier." She scooped again, weighed it, and wrote the numbers in her notebook. Packed cup, big number. Fluffed cup, smaller number. Every single time.

"Scooping straight from the bag packs it down," Grace said slowly, reading her own notes. "So my cup is holding way more flour than the recipe wants. That's why they're dry and cakey." She flipped to a clean page. "Grandma, does your recipe book have weights?"

"Top of every page, honey. Bakers weigh flour because it's more accurate."

Grace measured everything by weight for the fourth batch, double-checking each number like a scientist. When she pulled the pan out, the cookies had spread into golden rounds with crackled tops, and the smell made her mouth water. She carried the plate to the porch where her cousins were waiting, and Grandpa announced that the lemonade was definitely not synthetic, squeezed from real lemons that morning.

"Try one," Grace said, holding out the plate with both hands. "I weighed the flour myself."

"Fourteen dollars for one bottle," Marcus said, holding his phone screen toward the seat behind him. "My cousin says AquaPure strips toxins out of your body in nine days. Look at the site. Lab coats, testimonials, everything."

Sophie leaned over the aisle of the rumbling bus and studied the page. It did look impressive: a doctor in a white coat, a chart climbing upward, paragraphs of glowing reviews. She scrolled a little and noticed a small link at the bottom, "Shop Now," and beneath it, in faint gray letters, the name of the company that owned the website. The same company, she saw, that sold the drink.

"That's weird," she said. "The people who made the site are the people selling it." She thought about that for a moment. Judging the site by its own pages felt like asking a used-car salesman whether his car ran well. He would say yes, whoever he was. What she needed was somebody outside the deal.

"Hey, Marcus, hand me your phone a second." She opened a new tab and typed the drink's name plus the word "scam." A news article from a consumer magazine appeared, then a doctor's blog, then a warning from a health agency. None of them had anything good to say. One called the "clinical study" an internal company document that nobody outside could verify. She opened two more tabs to be sure, and the story from outside the site was the same everywhere.

"So it's fake?" Marcus groaned. "I already told my cousin I'd advocate for it at lunch. He gets a cut if we sell six bottles."

"Wait, what's this called, opening other tabs instead of trusting the site itself?" said Priya from the window seat, looking over Sophie's shoulder.

"Lateral reading," Sophie said. "My sister says professionals do it that way."

"Well, you just saved me fourteen dollars," Marcus said. He tapped out a message to his cousin, then frowned at his phone. "He's going to be mad."

"He'll survive," Priya said. "Tell him to read the magazine article."

"I will." Marcus slumped back, then straightened up. "Okay, but my cousin also says our principal used to be in a monarchy's royal guard, and that's why he walks so stiff. Is that checkable or is that just an opinion?"

Sophie laughed. "Whether he was a royal guard is a claim you could check, if you can find records. Whether he walks stiff is just what your cousin thinks." She opened a fresh tab. "Give me his full name."

Marcus spelled it out, and Priya scooted over to share the screen as the bus turned the last corner toward school.

"You can't cancel a trip we've been planning since October," Priya typed back. "My mom already bought the giant umbrella."

"Did you read this?" Marcus sent the link again, as if nobody had seen it the first time. "He needed forty stitches. FORTY."

Caleb frowned at his screen. He had read the story, and it was gross, and the detail about the stitches was going to stick in his brain like gum on a shoe. But something about it bothered him. They called it the availability heuristic."

"That sounds like a dinosaur," Marcus replied.

"It means people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind," Caleb typed. "One shark story jumps into your head because it's scary and vivid, so your brain says, see, it happens all the time. It doesn't."

Priya sent a thinking emoji. "Wait, that's why my grandma thinks all restaurants in other countries will poison her. She saw one news story about bad Mexican cuisine in 1998."

"Exactly," Caleb wrote. "That's the same thing happening."

Marcus's typing bubble appeared, vanished, appeared again. Finally he sent: "Okay but the ocean is dark and I would feel extremely vulnerable out there. Also I still want to go on the trip, I just want to sit on the sand and be hilarious, which is my job."

"Your job is carrying the cooler," Priya said.

"Fine. The cooler AND being hilarious."

"Deal," Caleb typed. "And if you get in the water up to your knees, I'll count that as a win. Baby steps. The shark in your head is way bigger than the real odds."

There was a long pause, and then Marcus sent one message: "Up to my knees. But if anything touches my leg, I'm launching straight out of the ocean like a dolphin and nobody gets to film it."

Priya replied, "No promises on the filming."
