story:
The tryout sheet in Theo's hand had one line left open: defense, second squad. He'd been at Pine Hollow Ice Arena since six in the morning, and his legs felt like wet rope, but he could still skate, so he lined up for the final drill. The coach blew the whistle, and Theo bent his knees and cut hard around the first cone, imagining that the cone was Eli Marsh, the fastest winger in the district. He couldn't mimic Eli's full speed, but he could copy the way the boy changed direction late,欺骗ing defenders. So far it was working.

Then it stopped working for somebody else. Marcus Boyd, a stocky kid Theo knew from science class, raced backward to catch a breakaway, tangled skates with a winger, and went down. His helmet cracked against the ice with a sound like a dropped coconut. He stood up too fast, swayed, and grabbed the boards. Theo skated over because he was closest, and because last year he had done the same thing himself.

"Get away, I'm fine," Marcus said, blinking hard at the scoreboard as if the numbers were moving. "There's like ten minutes left. If I sit out, I don't make the team."

Theo remembered his own eighth-grade soccer tryout, when he'd bounced his head off a goalpost and stayed in because he was afraid of exactly that. He'd felt strange for two days, and his mother had been furious, and even now he couldn't decide whether staying in had been brave or just reckless. He had scored, though. That part he still thought about.

"Sit down a second," Theo said. "There's a rule about this. My uncle told me. It's called the Zackery Lystedt Law. Washington passed it in 2009, and it was the first state law in the country like it. If they even think you have a concussion, you're out until a doctor or somebody clears you." Marcus lowered himself onto the bench, still arguing, saying it was just a bump, that his whole body felt twisted up like a knot of intestine. Theo waved the coach over anyway.

The coach crouched in front of Marcus, looked at his eyes, and pulled the clipboard off the boards. "He's done for today," she told the assistant. "Protocol." Marcus put his head in his gloves.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Marcus was quiet for a long moment, helmet dangling from one finger. "Do you think I still have a shot? There's another tryout Thursday."

"There's a whole season after that," Theo said. "There's nothing after your brain."

Marcus snorted, then winced and touched his temple. "Okay. But if they take you instead of me, I'm blaming the law."

story:
Romy pushed through the metal door of the Riverside Food Bank with a box of granola bars her mom had bought by mistake, thinking they were for school snacks. Inside she expected a line of people waiting for food, maybe folding tables and grocery bags. Instead she found a warehouse, plain and enormous, with pallets stacked to the rafters and a forklift beeping somewhere in the back. No customers anywhere. Just a woman in a green apron counting cans into a spreadsheet.

"You're early," the woman said. "Distribution's not here."

"Where is it?" Romy asked, because obviously it had to be somewhere. People didn't come to a warehouse to shop. Nobody wanted to walk past a forklift for a bag of rice.

The woman, whose name tag said DEB, pointed her pencil toward the door. "The pantry on Fourth Street. That's where people pick up their groceries directly. This is the food bank. We collect and store the large amounts first, then truck them out." She squinted at Romy's box. "You volunteering or just delivering?"

"Volunteering," Romy said, though she had only signed up because her friend Priya had bailed and Romy had already told her mom she'd gone.

Deb's own plan soon became clear. She wanted to finish inventory before her daughter's soccer game at noon, and she kept glancing at the clock like it might sneak ahead. "You can count soup or you can sort the eccentric donations bin," she said. "Somebody donated a hundred cans of pickled okra and one birdbath."

Romy chose the bin. The birdbath turned out to be ceramic, heavy, and inexplicably painted with the face of a cat. She carried it to the corner where the odd donations lived, next to a bag of hotel shampoos and a trombone mouthpiece.

Then she noticed something. The pasta shelf had a gap, and the gap had a shape: long, straight, and exactly the width of spaghetti boxes. On the far wall, the spaghetti boxes sat in a pallet, forty of them, waiting to be moved. Romy had an idea. If the warehouse stored large amounts and sent them out to smaller places, then whatever left the shelves fastest was whatever people actually needed most. The pasta gap was wide. The pickled okra pile was not moving at all.

She tested it by asking Deb, casually, which orders went out that morning. "Spaghetti, peanut butter, canned peaches," Deb said without looking up. "Nobody wants the okra. The pantry on Fourth has a whole shelf of it."

So the pattern held. The shelves were like footprints showing where the food would go next, and Romy spent the next hour counting the gaps instead of just the cans, calling out the low ones so Deb could mark them for the next truck. Deb finished her spreadsheet at eleven forty, ten minutes before the soccer game, and patted the cat-faced birdbath on her way out.

"Take the okra if you want it," she said. "Consider it a conservation effort. We've got to conserve shelf space somehow."

Romy carried home three cans and the trombone mouthpiece, which nobody had claimed. The mouthpiece turned out to fit nothing in her house, but it made an excellent, brass-toned doorstop, and every time she tripped over it she thought of the cat birdbath, still standing in the corner, waiting for its own truck to Fourth Street.

story:
Oliver sat in the waiting room with his shirt held out from his armpits, sniffing each side like a detective at a crime scene. Both sides smelled like gym socks that had been locked in a locker over summer vacation. Three weeks ago they hadn't. That was the mystery. He had used the same soap, worn the same shirts, played the same sports, and suddenly, at his eleven-year checkup, he was sitting in the corner seat farthest from the other patients, holding his elbows tight against his ribs.

In the chair beside him, his sixteen-year-old cousin Marco flipped through a magazine about dirt bikes. He had driven Oliver because Mom's car was in the shop. "You keep doing that sniffing thing," Marco said. "You look like a golden retriever."

"Something changed," Oliver said. "I want to know what. I used to be immune to stink. I could run five laps and smell like nothing."

Marco put down the magazine. "Fresh sweat doesn't really have a smell, you know. The stink comes later. Bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from glands in your armpits, and those glands switch on around your age."

Oliver considered this. So the sweat itself was innocent. The bacteria were the culprits. That meant the crime scene was under his arms, and the evidence needed time to develop, like the smell in Marco's hockey bag. It also meant there was a way to test it.

In the exam room, the doctor checked his ears, his knees, and his growth chart, and said he was doing fine. On the way out, Oliver stopped at the drinking fountain and wet a paper towel, then ducked into the bathroom and scrubbed one armpit with soap from the dispenser. The other one he left alone. A scientific control, like in fourth grade. He dried off, rejoined Marco, and rode home with his arms at his sides, breathing through his nose and taking notes in his head.

At home he checked every hour. The washed side stayed plain and unremarkable, like tap water. The unwashed side grew steadily worse, like a sandwich left in a hot car. By dinner he had eliminated every other possible cause. New shirts, no. Different food, no. It was bacteria working on sweat, and the smell took time, exactly as Marco had said. He reported his findings at the table, and his little sister set down her fork and announced she was moving to the garage.

The next morning Oliver used Mom's deodorant from the cabinet above the sink, then walked to school with his arms swinging loose for the first time in weeks. Marcus, who sat next to him in third period, leaned over during attendance and said, "You smell like my dad's gym bag, but in a good way."

"I'll take it," Oliver said. "That's called data."

story:
Mrs. Okafor's office smelled like lemon tea, and a poster on the wall showed a cartoon brain holding a red umbrella. Ivy sat on the squishy blue chair by the window, watching the door, because her brother Devon was supposed to arrive at three fifteen and it was already three eighteen. Her plan for today was simple: convince Mrs. Okafor that Devon needed help before his science presentation on Thursday, the one he had already tried to skip twice by claiming he was sick.

When Devon finally slid in, his backpack strap was twisted and his face was pale. Ivy had noticed a pattern at home. He was fine all morning, cheerful even, and then around first period he would go quiet, and by the time he had to speak in front of anyone his hands shook. "He had to give a book report last month," she told Mrs. Okafor. "His heart was pounding like he'd run a mile, and he was breathing fast, and nothing was even happening. Nothing dangerous, I mean. It was just a book report."

Devon glared at the umbrella poster. "That was one time," he said, but his voice wobbled, which illustrated the point better than anything Ivy could add. Mrs. Okafor asked him what the worst part was. "The humiliation," Devon said quietly. "Everyone looking at me like I'm going to throw up."

"Here's what I keep reading," Mrs. Okafor said, turning her chair toward him. "It's called fight-or-flight." Devon frowned, so Ivy leaned forward. "What's that?" Mrs. Okafor said it was the body getting ready for danger, and that during fight-or-flight the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up. Ivy sat back. So Devon's body was doing exactly what bodies were built to do. It wasn't broken. It was just loud.

"So it's like a smoke alarm," Ivy said, testing the idea out loud. "It's not a fire. The alarm doesn't know that." Devon chewed on the thought. Mrs. Okafor nodded slowly and mentioned that lots of kids called that feeling anxiety, that stress had a way of turning up the alarm, and that coping skills were basically ways to tell the alarm to settle down. She also said the word boundaries, about Devon telling classmates he'd answer questions after class instead of during, but Ivy was already forming a plan of her own.

"Then let's practice," she said, standing up. She pointed Devon toward the window, where three kids were crossing the parking lot below. "Pretend they're your class. Give your presentation to them. If your heart starts pounding, that's just the adrenaline, and you keep going anyway." Devon exhaled, rolled his shoulders, and faced the glass. "Photosynthesis," he began, "is how plants make their own food." His voice cracked on the second word, and he kept talking anyway. Ivy sat down to listen, and Mrs. Okafor wrote resilient on her notepad, underlined it twice, and slid it across the desk where Devon could see it when he finished.

story:
Victor stabbed his fork into a meatball and pushed it around the plate while his little sister talked with her mouth full of noodles. Everyone at the table was doing that thing where they pretended to eat normally, but really they were all sneaking glances at the trading card he had propped against the salt shaker. It was a Blazetail Dragon, foil edition, and three days ago nobody at Jefferson Middle School would have traded a broken pencil for it.

"Now everyone wants one," his mother said, reaching over to turn the card so it caught the light. "How much did Damon offer you today?"

"His skateboard, his hockey jersey, and forty dollars." Victor could still hear the cafeteria noise around that offer, half the seventh grade crowding the table, someone chanting "foil, foil" until a monitor told them to sit down. "Last month I bought it for two bucks at the garage sale by the library. Two bucks. Because nobody wanted it then."

His grandfather set down his spoon. "Two dollars. And now forty plus a skateboard." He smiled like he was remembering a joke he had played on himself a long time ago. "You know, I did a report on this in school. Not cards. Tulips." He let the word sit there while Grandma rolled her eyes and said, here we go. "In the Dutch Republic, in the winter of 1636 into 1637, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared. People were trading houses for a single bulb. And then in February 1637, it all collapsed, because buyers stopped showing up." He picked up his water glass. "One morning there was no one left to sell to. Just like that."

Victor stopped chewing. He thought about the hallway that afternoon, how he had counted six kids clutching Blazetail Dragons in plastic sleeves, and how Bruno had quietly tried to sell his for ten dollars and gotten no takers. Six dragons. Maybe there were more in lockers. The cafeteria had felt contagious that week, everyone wanting the card because everyone else wanted it, but wanting wasn't the same as there being enough to go around. Or too many. His stomach did a slow flip.

"I almost traded it," he said. "Yesterday. Marcus offered me his whole dinosaur fossil collection for it, and I said I'd think about it." He remembered standing at his window last night, holding the card up to the streetlight, feeling like a genius. Now he felt like the last person at a party who hadn't heard that everyone else had gone home. "What do I do?"

"That's not for me to say," his grandfather said, and Grandma squeezed Victor's hand and said something about how a smart boy figures out what a thing is worth when the crowd goes quiet. Her compassion, Victor thought, was mostly aimed at Marcus and his fossils.

That night, after the dishes, Victor sat at his desk with the card flat under his palm. He could keep it because he loved the way the foil turned green at an angle, or he could take it to school tomorrow and be the first seller in a room full of them. Downstairs, his sister was already asking if she could have it if he didn't want it anymore. He slid the card into a plain white envelope and wrote one word on the outside: "Wait."

story:
The marble soldier at the war memorial had one hand shading his eyes, looking west, as if he could see everything Evelyn could not. She sat on the bottom step with a photocopied settler's diary spread across her knees. Her project was due tomorrow morning, and the whole thing depended on one question: why had the Halloran family left Ohio in 1846? The diary said they wanted land of their own. But her teacher had written a note in red pen: "How do you know the diary is telling the truth?"

Her grandfather found her there after his walk, out of breath from the hill. "Still stuck?" He lowered himself onto the step beside her.

"The diary says a hailstorm ruined their crop on June 9th, so they gave up and left," Evelyn said. "But I found a newspaper from that same town, and it says the big hailstorm was in July." She turned the pages of the diary, her frustration growing acute. "The paper even printed a letter about it from a farmer two miles from the Hallorans. Same storm, different month."

"Which one is wrong?" her grandfather asked.

"That's the problem. I can't tell. I only have two things, and they disagree." She stared at the carved soldier. Then she flipped to the back of the folder, where she'd copied a page from the county government records. The Hallorans sold their land on June 2nd, a week before the diary's supposed hailstorm. She read it twice. "They sold the farm before the storm even happened. The storm can't be why they left."

"So the diary got the date wrong," her grandfather said.

"Or the diary got the whole reason wrong, and they wrote the storm in later to explain it." She sat back. The probability that the diary's date was right seemed small now, with two other sources pointing the other way. "I kept thinking the diary was automatically true because it was written by somebody who was there."

"You could write that," he said. "Show how you checked it."

The light was going orange behind the memorial when she began to write her new first paragraph. Letters, newspapers, government records: she listed them in her notebook like witnesses, each one confirming a piece of the story. The diary still mattered, but it had to answer to the others. When she finished the paragraph, she read it aloud to her grandfather and the stone soldier.

"That works," her grandfather said. "Now let's get you home before dark." Evelyn packed her folder, then looked back once at the soldier gazing west, toward all that land the Hallorans had gone chasing after all.

"Green Arrow is the fastest car in this whole neighborhood," Declan announced, holding the lime-green car over his head. "Maybe the fastest in the county."

Oliver looked at the ramp they had built against the fence, a long board propped on the old picnic table. Green Arrow had just beaten Oliver's red car, Falcon, by what looked like half a car length. One race. Half a car length.

"That was one race," Oliver said.

"One race that Green Arrow won," Declan said, as if that settled it. He was already lining the cars up again, but this time Oliver stopped him.

"Hang on." Oliver picked up a stick and scratched two columns in the dirt at the bottom of the ramp, one marked G, one marked F. "We race them five times. We count the wins. Then we know."

"We already know," Declan said. "My dad said he'd bet the mortgage on Green Arrow." Oliver's own dad said stuff like that too, usually right before losing the weekly card game to Aunt Rhonda.

"That's not knowing, that's bragging," Oliver said. "Think of it like this. We can't see which car is really faster. It's hidden. So we make a guess we can test. My guess is that Falcon wins more than half the time."

"That's a weird way to say 'I think I'll win,'" Declan said, but he set the cars on the top of the ramp anyway. "Ready? Let go."

They let go together. Green Arrow pulled ahead halfway down and won by two car lengths. Oliver scratched a tally mark under G.

Race two went to Falcon. Race three went to Falcon too, barely, a nose ahead at the flowerpot finish line. Declan crouched down and squinted at the wheels of Green Arrow, spinning them with his thumb. Race four, Green Arrow. Race five, Falcon. The score stood at three to two, Falcon.

"Best out of five," Oliver said. "Falcon wins."

"Rematch," Declan said instantly. "Best out of five again. Different dirt."

So they ran it again. Falcon took three out of five the second time too. On the third set, Green Arrow won the first two races and Declan did a small dance in the grass, but Falcon came back and took the set, three to two again. Same score, three sets in a row.

"That's weird," Declan said, staring at the tally marks scratched across the dirt. "It's the same every time."

"It's consistent," Oliver said. "That's how we know it's real. If we'd only raced once, the first time, Green Arrow won, remember? You'd still be doing your county speech." He pointed at the mark under G. "One race can go either way. It could just be luck. But when it keeps coming out the same over and over, that means something."

Declan sat back on his heels. "So how much faster is Falcon? Like, a lot?"

"We could try to quantify it," Oliver said. "Measure the gaps. My mom has a tape measure in the garage."

Declan was already running toward the garage. "If Falcon loses the measuring, I'm calling for a fourth rematch!"

"Bring the pencil too," Oliver called after him. "And a rag, your car's got mud in its wheel wells."

story:
Nora spread her survey results across the lab table and tapped her pencil on the edge of the sink. Thirty-two students had answered her question, and the pattern was hard to miss: kids who ate breakfast almost all had better grades than kids who skipped it. Her poster board, half finished, already said "Eat Breakfast, Get Better Grades," in fat blue letters. She had planned to glue on the graph during lunch, but something about the headline was bothering her.

Desmond leaned over from the next table, where he was adjusting the valve on his Bunsen burner. The flame had been sputtering, and when he turned the knob a fraction, it steadied into a neat blue cone. "That's a good graph," he said. "My project is so boring compared to yours. I just burned three kinds of chips."

"It looks good," Nora admitted. "But watch this." She picked up her data sheet and read down the breakfast column. "Tomas doesn't eat breakfast and he gets D's. Priya eats breakfast every day and gets A's." She paused. "But Tomas's family also moved twice this year, and he stays up past midnight. Priya's house is quiet, and she sleeps nine hours." The more she stared at her sheet, the more pairs like that she found. The breakfast skippers were also the kids with long bus rides and lumpy schedules.

"That still counts, doesn't it?" Desmond asked. "They go together."

Nora remembered a word from a science article she had read for the project, and she said it out loud to test it. "Correlation. Two things happening together." Then she added slowly, "But going together doesn't prove one causes the other. Something else might cause both." Tomas's messy mornings and his D's could both come from the same unsettled year, no cereal required. She felt her shoulders drop, relieved rather than defeated, because now she actually had a question worth asking.

She pulled out a fresh sheet of paper and wrote a new survey, one that asked about sleep, bus rides, and homework time along with breakfast. Mr. Okafor walked past and glanced at her revision, but he only raised an eyebrow and kept moving, which she took as a legitimate sign she was on the right track. By the time the bell rang, her poster headline had changed to "Breakfast and Grades: Which Comes First?" and beneath it she had drawn two arrows meeting at a mystery box with a question mark inside. Desmond peered over as he snapped off his burner, and the flame ceased with a soft pop. "So what's in the box?" he asked. "I don't know yet," Nora said, and picked up her pencil again.

The box from his uncle arrived on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday, Nolan was holding a phone for the first time in his life. It was Uncle Dev's old one, passed down with a crack in the corner and a battery that didn't seem to last. Nolan plugged it in overnight, carried it to school on Thursday, and watched it die right after lunch. He told himself it was a fluke. Friday it died during fifth period, before lunch even started.

That night, sprawled on his bed, Nolan typed into the family group chat, which Mom had named "Vasquez HQ." Phone keeps dying by lunch. Is it broken? Uncle Dev replied first with a thumbs-up and then, a minute later, actual words: Not broken. Old. It's a lithium-ion battery, and as it chemically ages it holds less charge. That phone's been through four years of me.

Nolan read the message three times. So the dying by lunchtime wasn't random, and it wasn't his fault, and it also wasn't going to stop. The battery would just keep holding less and less. He started a notes file and tracked it like a science experiment: Saturday, 46 percent by noon. Sunday, 41 percent. The numbers slid downward in a steady line, which meant Monday would be worse, and Mom's birthday dinner was Monday night. He had promised to film her blowing out the candles, and he had a suspicion the phone wouldn't survive until dessert.

He remembered, with a squirm of guilt, the argument in August when he'd said he didn't need a charger in his room because he'd "be careful." He'd thought careful meant immune to stuff like this. Now he understood that being careful had nothing to do with a battery slowly wearing out on its own schedule, whether he deserved it or not. He typed: Dev, do you still have that portable battery pack from the camping trip?

His uncle left it on the porch the next morning inside a plastic bag, along with a sticky note that said, No take-backs. At Monday's dinner, Nolan kept the phone plugged into the pack in his jacket pocket, feeling the small warm weight of it through the fabric like a secret plan. When the cake came out, he propped the phone against the salt shaker and hit record. His mom laughed at the lens, his little sister dove in front of it, and the battery icon held at 38 percent all the way through the candles.

Later, he posted the video in Vasquez HQ with the caption, Evidence that this phone can make it through a whole evening. Uncle Dev replied within seconds: Empathy, kid. I lost plenty of birthday videos to that thing. Nolan started to type back something about trading the phone in eventually, then stopped, thumb hovering, and left the words unsent. He scrolled up instead and watched his mom blow out the candles one more time.

story:
The arena smelled like cold rubber and hot pretzels, and Aaron's whole row of family and friends had turned into one loud, scarf-wrapped blob. His cousin Maya elbowed him every time the home team's defenseman, a big kid named Ruiz with a predatory grin, chased down a breakaway. "Watch him," Maya said. "He hunts pucks like a shark." Aaron's grandpa sat on the other side, wrapped in a coat thick enough to insulate a polar explorer, though the rink was barely cold at all.

Then the disputed goal happened. The puck vanished behind a pile of skates, the goal light flashed, and half the arena screamed while the other half booed. "It never crossed the line!" shouted Uncle Theo. "It did so!" shouted Aunt Regina, and they both leaned toward the jumbotron like it was the last cookie on the plate.

The screen showed the play again, slowed down. That was when Grandpa snorted. "You know, TV couldn't always do that. The first time instant replay was used in a live sports broadcast was by CBS director Tony Verna, during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963."

"Wait," Aaron said. "Before that, people just argued forever?"

"Forever," Grandpa said, "with no proof but loudness."

Aaron grinned, but his mind had already snagged on something else. In the replay, the net looked wrong. Crooked. He couldn't see the puck, but he could see the net's mooring peg, that little thing that holds the goal in place, floating loose on the ice beside the post. His idea: if the net had come off its peg before the shot, the goal might not count even if the puck went in, because a displaced net changes what counts. He grabbed Maya's arm. "Look at the peg. Look at it."

Maya squinted. "The little orange thingy? It's just... sitting there. Like a lost sock."

"On the next replay, watch the post," Aaron said. The screen rolled the play again, and there it was, clear as anything: a defender crashed the crease a full second before the shot, the peg popped loose, and the net slid sideways just enough to swallow the puck. The referee skated to the penalty box, pointed, and waved off the goal. The scoreboard blinked: NO GOAL, NET OFF MOORINGS.

Uncle Theo stood up and bowed to Aaron like he was royalty. Aunt Regina threw a popcorn kernel at him, but she was laughing.

Above them, the big ceiling fan spun with a low hum like a turbine winding up, and the Zamboni rumbled out through the tunnel for intermission. Aaron sat back, satisfied. "See?" he told Maya. "You don't always need to see the puck. Sometimes you just need to see what moved."

"Fine, detective," Maya said. "Next period, tell me where the pretzel guy went, because that one I actually care about."
